definition: Coercion is external pressure or influence that interferes with a person’s free choice, such as pushing or inducing someone to cast a particular vote. In this context, it also includes situations that enable vote-selling rather than an independent decision.

reasons: The packet does not define coercion as “external pressure or influence that interferes with a person’s free choice”; it only discusses “coercion-resistance” as a security property preventing “external influence.”
The packet does not provide examples like “pushing or inducing someone to cast a particular vote.”

While the packet mentions “vote-selling” as a concern addressed by “coercion-resistance,” it does not explicitly frame this as “situations that enable vote-selling rather than an independent decision,” so that part is not supported by the packet.

The packet supports coercion as external influence in e-voting, but it does not support the added claim that coercion “includes situations that enable vote-selling rather than an independent decision.”
The vote-selling language in the packet appears only as part of the description of coercion-resistance, not as a definition of coercion itself.
